name: No rules

why: 'satisfied' with question 1 answered no. If question 1 were yes, question 2 would have to be yes and no. A method that guesses yes and never takes a guess back returns None here.

why: 'satisfied'. The implication graph has 100,000 vertices and 200,000 edges; one search for groups, O(n + m).

name: A forced chain of 50,000
expr: sat_check(args[0], args[1], two_sat(args[0], [tuple(c) for c in args[1]]))
why: 'satisfied': every question is forced to yes. The implication graph is a path 100,000 vertices long, so the search must not use recursion.

name: A chain of 50,000 that closes
expr: sat_check(args[0], args[1], two_sat(args[0], [tuple(c) for c in args[1]]))
why: 'no assignment'. Now every vertex of the implication graph is in one group of 100,000, so question 1's yes and no are in the same group.

name: A chain that forbids the last
expr: sat_check(args[0], args[1], two_sat(args[0], [tuple(c) for c in args[1]]))
why: 'satisfied': every question answered no. A method that tries yes for question 1, follows what it forces to the end of the chain, finds the clash and starts again for question 2, and so on, does about n²/2 = 1,250,000,000 steps. The implication graph does one search.
